Let's talk about how much building work you're actually allowed to do — because this is where a lot of Class Q schemes fall apart. The right lets you convert the building, and it gives you a short, closed list of works to do it with: new windows, doors, a roof, external walls, the services — water, drainage, electricity — and just enough partial demolition to carry those out. That's it. If a job isn't on that list, it doesn't matter how sensible it is, it's outside the Class. And even the works that are on the list have to go no further than the conversion genuinely needs. The key line the guidance draws is this: you can't build new structural elements. If the building can't take the conversion without a new frame, new load-bearing walls, or effectively rebuilding it, then what you're doing isn't a conversion at all.

And that's really the whole battleground, so let me give you the case it all turns on — Hibbitt. Picture a steel-framed farm building, largely open on three sides, barely any cladding. The owner wanted to turn it into a house; it was refused, and the court backed the refusal. The principle that came out of it is the one to carry with you: Class Q permits a conversion, but not works so major that, in practical reality, what you're really doing is a rebuild, or a new build from scratch. And here's the subtle part — it's judged as a whole. Even if you can point at each individual operation and say, well, that one's on the list, if the totality of what you're doing amounts to reconstruction, the whole scheme falls outside the Class. The starting point has to be a building that's genuinely capable of being converted in the first place.

So, practically? Open-sided, skeletal, half-derelict barns are poor candidates, and no amount of clever drafting fixes that. And don't be tempted to understate the works to sneak through prior approval — because anything you build beyond what's permitted is simply unlawful, whatever the approval letter says. This is exactly why the structural engineer's report earns its money. It has to speak to capability, not just condition — can this building actually be converted using only the permitted works? If the honest answer involves underpinning, new foundations, or replacing the frame, that's your signal to stop and go for a full planning application instead. Trying to force it through Class Q just buys you an enforcement problem down the line.
